analysis.one_liner: Exempts big local phone companies from most network-sharing and price rules on new broadband networks.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors, the bill got one Senate hearing but never a committee vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would free the big incumbent local phone companies from most 1996 Telecom Act rules on their new broadband networks: no requirement to share newly deployed fiber or packet-based equipment with competitors, no price regulation of advanced services where an unaffiliated provider also offers one, and no obligation to pay for carrying traffic to the Internet or to ISPs [S2] [S3]. In exchange, carriers would have to make advanced service available to 80% of a state's customers within three years, and to any requesting customer within five years, or forfeit the relief [S2]. The bill received one hearing in the Senate Commerce Committee and never a vote before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Incumbent local exchange carriers — the dominant regional phone companies — gain if the bill passes: they would be freed from 1996 Telecom Act duties to interconnect and lease network elements for packet-based and fiber networks, freed from price regulation on advanced services wherever an unaffiliated provider competes, and freed from paying for transport and termination of traffic to the Internet [S2]. As a condition, they must make advanced service available to 80% of a state's customers within three years and to any requesting customer within five, or lose the relief [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: For the incumbent carriers it targets, the bill removes 1996 Act duties to interconnect with competitors and lease network elements on packet-based networks, new fiber runs, and related premises, freeing those investments from mandated sharing [S2] [S3].

It promises consumers a buildout: each incumbent must offer advanced service to 80% of a state's customers within three years and to any requesting customer within five years, on pain of losing the regulatory relief [S2] [S3].

It gives carriers price flexibility for advanced services wherever an unaffiliated provider offers advanced service in the same exchange, with petitions deemed approved if the FCC does not act within 30 days [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Competitive local exchange carriers and independent ISPs bear the cost: they lose court-enforced access to newly deployed fiber and packet-based network elements, lose unbundled access except for elements used mostly for ordinary phone service, and stop receiving payments for terminating traffic to the Internet [S3]. Consumers in areas without a competing advanced-service provider would face advanced-service prices with only a filed schedule rather than regulation [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Competing phone carriers and independent ISPs

drawbacks.text: The consumer-facing buildout deadlines are heavily qualified: they apply only where advanced service can be provided 'using an industry-approved standard and existing loop facilities,' giving carriers a built-in argument that a missed deadline is not enforceable [S2] [S3].

The bill removes incumbent carriers' obligation to pay for transport, delivery, or termination of telecommunications to the Internet or any ISP, ending payments independent ISPs received and reclassifying such traffic as interstate under exclusive FCC jurisdiction [S2] [S3].
It narrows unbundling to elements used predominantly for telephone exchange service, shrinking the cost-based access to incumbent networks on which competitive carriers were built [S3].

Pricing relief is effectively automatic: a petition is deemed approved if the FCC does not act within 30 days, and advanced service outside a carrier's 1996 home territory is exempt from both federal and state regulation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill frames itself as a trade: lighter regulation in exchange for broadband buildout deadlines. But the deadlines carry a loophole — they bind only where service can be delivered with an existing standard and existing loop facilities — and the pricing-relief process defaults to approval if the FCC does not respond in 30 days [S3]. The clearest, immediate gains go to the incumbent phone companies, while the costs fall on the competitors and ISPs that the 1996 Act's access rules were designed to protect; consumers would benefit from buildout only if the deadlines prove enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: It never left the Senate Commerce Committee — a hearing was held in July 2000, no vote was ever taken, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Introduced July 20, 2000, and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The committee held a hearing on July 26, 2000 (printed as S.Hrg. 106-1139) but took no further action on the bill.
No senator joined as a cosponsor, including from either party.
The bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Competitive local carriers and independent ISPs are better off because the bill died: the 1996 Act rules that gave them access to incumbent networks at regulated terms stayed in place. Broadband customers kept the existing open-access framework and the regulatory backstop over incumbent prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Competing carriers, ISPs, and broadband customers

for.name: Sen. Sam Brownback
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 20, 2000, as its sole sponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Commerce Committee.

for.name: Regional Bell operating companies
for.what_they_did: Campaigning for broadband deregulation of incumbent phone networks through companion measures like this bill and the House's Tauzin-Dingell bill.

against.name: Competitive telecommunications carriers and independent internet service providers
against.role: Competitive telecom carriers and independent ISPs
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed Bell-company broadband deregulation, arguing it would let incumbents strand competitors and shutter independent ISPs.

sides.party_line_note: There were no roll calls and no cosponsors; the bill was introduced by a single Republican and never advanced, so no party-line split ever formed.

industries.industry: Incumbent local telephone companies (regional Bell carriers)
industries.note: The bill's centerpiece is regulatory relief for these carriers on their broadband networks: no duty to share new fiber or packet equipment, pricing flexibility, and no payments for Internet-traffic termination [S2] [S3]. The offsetting buildout deadlines are qualified by whether service 'can be provided using an industry-approved standard and existing loop facilities.'

industries.industry: Competitive local exchange carriers and DSL competitors
industries.note: These carriers' business models under the 1996 Telecom Act depend on leasing incumbent network elements at regulated rates; the bill removes that access for packet-based and fiber elements and most unbundling, directly undercutting DSL and data competitors [S2] [S3].

The bill bars any requirement that carriers pay for transport, delivery, or termination of traffic to the Internet or ISPs, ending reciprocal-compensation revenue many independent ISPs relied on and shifting those costs [S2] [S3].
